question:
Patient note:
A 66-year-old man, formerly employed as a city bus mechanic and right-hand dominant, came to the outpatient neurology rehabilitation service this morning accompanied by his sister for reassessment of persistent right-sided weakness and increasing flexor tone in the arm that have limited his ability to handle small tools and dress independently. Nine months earlier he was admitted to another hospital with sudden onset of expressive aphasia, right facial droop, and dense paresis of the right upper and lower extremities; brain MRI at that time demonstrated an acute left middle cerebral artery infarction involving both cortical and subcortical territories, and he received intravenous alteplase within two hours of symptom recognition. He spent a week on a dedicated stroke unit followed by four weeks of inpatient rehabilitation, then transitioned to thrice-weekly outpatient physical and occupational therapy, which he has continued without interruption. Speech has largely recovered—he converses fluently and follows complex instructions—yet motor recovery has plateaued: the right shoulder abducts only against gravity, elbow flexion is 2/5, wrist extension is trace, intrinsic hand muscles are flaccid, and the right leg generates enough strength to bear partial weight with a knee-ankle-foot orthosis but cannot clear the toe during swing phase; he walks ten meters in therapy sessions with a platform walker and maximal assistance, otherwise relies on a lightweight manual wheelchair for community mobility. The left side demonstrates full strength and normal tone. He denies memory lapses, getting lost in familiar surroundings, or difficulty managing his finances; his sister confirms that he still pays household bills online and recalls recent news events. Prior to the stroke he had no history of transient chest tightness, diaphoresis, emergent catheterization, or lower-extremity edema, and since discharge he has ambulated short household distances without dyspnea, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal breathing difficulty. Remote health records note borderline fasting glucose values discovered three years ago (106–112 mg/dL) for which he adopted a Mediterranean-style diet and lost 5 kg; last week’s laboratory panel showed hemoglobin A1c 5.8 % and fasting plasma glucose 101 mg/dL, and he has never taken metformin or other antihyperglycemics. He reports no episodes of calf pain with walking, non-healing lower-extremity ulcerations, color changes in the feet, or diminished pedal pulses on prior examinations. Respiratory history is unremarkable: he never smoked, has not carried inhalers, was never told of asthma or emphysema, and chest imaging performed during the initial hospitalization showed clear lung fields with normal diaphragms. Gastrointestinal review is negative for epigastric burning, early satiety, hematemesis, melena, or iron-deficiency anemia, and he recalls no prior endoscopies. He does not drink alcohol, denies injection drug use, and screening serologies six months ago were negative for viral hepatitis; serial comprehensive metabolic panels have revealed aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 26 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. Serum creatinine this visit is 0.9 mg/dL with estimated glomerular filtration rate 85 mL/min/1.73 m², and urinalysis shows no protein or hematuria. There is no personal or family history of leukemia, lymphoma, solid organ malignancy, or immunodeficiency, and age-appropriate colonoscopy two years ago revealed only small hyperplastic polyps. Current medications include aspirin 81 mg daily, high-intensity atorvastatin 40 mg nightly initiated for secondary vascular prevention, baclofen 10 mg three times daily for spasticity, and vitamin D 1000 IU daily; he is allergic to penicillin, which caused a rash decades ago. He abstains from herbal supplements and consumes one cup of coffee each morning. Vital signs obtained in clinic: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 122/70 mm Hg seated in the left arm, heart rate 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air; body mass index is 24 kg/m². On examination he is alert, oriented, and conversant. Carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, jugular venous pulsation measures 4 cm above the sternal angle, and the point of maximal impulse is in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line without heave. Heart sounds are crisp S1 and S2 with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout with equal expansion and no wheezes or crackles. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, with normal bowel sounds, a liver edge palpable at the costal margin but smooth, and no splenomegaly or ascites. Pulses are 2+ in radial, femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries bilaterally, capillary refill is under two seconds, and there are no trophic skin changes. Neurologic examination confirms intact cranial nerves II through XII, right upper-limb strength 1/5 proximally and 0/5 distally, right lower-limb strength 2/5 at hip flexors and knee extensors with spastic catch, sustained ankle clonus on the right, brisk reflexes and an upgoing plantar response on that side, while the left limbs exhibit 5/5 power, normal tone, and flexor plantar responses. Light-touch and pin-prick sensation are diminished in a glove-and-stocking distribution on the right but preserved on the left; proprioception is intact in both great toes. Coordination testing of the left hand is normal, but rapid alternating movements cannot be performed on the right. Gait assessment shows wheelchair propulsion with good left-arm drive; when assisted to stand, he bears 60 % body weight through the right leg but requires considerable support for balance. Skin inspection reveals no pressure ulcers. A follow-up non-contrast head CT obtained last week to rule out hydrocephalus shows the expected area of left fronto-parietal encephalomalacia without new hemorrhage or mass effect. The patient seeks guidance on optimizing tone management, exploring functional electrical stimulation options, and understanding long-term cardiovascular risk while planning a return to part-time desk work within the coming year.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI): add the age points and the weights of qualifying conditions.
- Age 66 falls in the 60–69 band: 2 points.
- Cerebrovascular disease: MRI confirmed a left middle cerebral artery infarct at admission: 1 point.
- Hemiplegia/hemiparesis: dense right arm and leg paresis was present before alteplase and persisted after rehabilitation: 2 points.
- Other CCI conditions: 0 points. Impaired fasting glucose is not diabetes, and no other qualifying disease is documented.
Counting both the infarct and the motor deficit, the sum is 2 + 1 + 2 + 0 = 5.
Final answer: 5
